blocks.text: Before anything else, a decision about words. The school we are about to study is known in Chinese as 唯識 (wéishì), and in English it is variously called "Mind-Only", "Consciousness-Only", "Representation-Only", or simply **Yogācāra** (瑜伽行派). These are not interchangeable, and the choice affects how a newcomer imagines the whole system. In these notes the main name is *Yogācāra*, with *Consciousness-Only* as its gloss, and *Mind-Only* is avoided except where we are quoting or discussing it. Here is why.

items: **What 唯識 translates.** Xuánzàng's 唯識 renders the Sanskrit **vijñapti-mātra** (or *vijñapti-mātratā*, "the state of being only vijñapti"). *Mātra* means "only, nothing but". *Vijñapti* is a causative form of the verb *vi-jñā*, "to discern, to know": literally, "that which makes known", a cognitive presentation or representation. So the most literal English is "nothing but representation" or "nothing but what consciousness presents". "Consciousness-only" is the conventional rendering, and it matches Xuánzàng's choice of 識 (*vijñāna*, consciousness) rather than 心 (*citta*, mind).

**Why not "Mind-Only"?** "Mind-only" properly translates a different Sanskrit phrase, **citta-mātra** (唯心), which appears in sūtras such as the *Daśabhūmika* ("the three realms are mind-only", 三界唯心) and the *Laṅkāvatāra*. Yogācāra authors do use *citta-mātra* too, but the technical slogan of the school is *vijñapti-mātra*. In English, "mind" also suggests one cosmic Mind behind everything, a reading that suits some later East Asian schools but not the Indian Yogācāra of this treatise, which analyses eight distinct consciousnesses, each arising moment by moment from its own seeds.

**Why "Yogācāra" first?** *Yogācāra* means "the practice of yoga", that is, of meditative discipline, and the treatise we are reading is the school's foundational text: the *Yogācārabhūmi*, "the stages of the yoga practitioner". The name tells us what the school is for. It grew out of meditators' experience, not out of armchair metaphysics, and its doctrines are meant to be verified in practice.

blocks.text: In short: *Yogācāra* names the school by its method; *Consciousness-Only* names it by its central claim. We use both, and we read "only" carefully, as the rest of this introduction explains.

secs.head: Where Yogācāra stands in Buddhist history

blocks.text: Yogācāra is one of the two great philosophical schools of Indian **Mahāyāna** (大乘) Buddhism. The other is **Madhyamaka** (中觀, the "Middle Way" school), founded by Nāgārjuna (龍樹) around the second century CE, which teaches that all phenomena are empty (śūnya, 空) of any fixed own-nature. Yogācāra appeared about two centuries later, in the fourth and fifth centuries, in north-west India.
Its founding figures, in the traditional account, are three:

items: **Maitreya** (彌勒), the future Buddha, then a bodhisattva dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, who taught the doctrine;
**Asaṅga** (無著), who received it from Maitreya and set it down in writing;

**Vasubandhu** (世親), Asaṅga's younger brother, who first wrote on Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma, was converted to the Mahāyāna by his brother, and composed the school's most concise statements, the *Twenty Verses* (《唯識二十論》) and the *Thirty Verses* (《唯識三十頌》).

blocks.text: After Vasubandhu came commentators such as Sthiramati (安慧) and Dharmapāla (護法), and the logicians Dignāga (陳那) and Dharmakīrti (法稱). At Nālandā, the great monastic university, Śīlabhadra (戒賢), a disciple of Dharmapāla, taught this tradition to the Chinese pilgrim **Xuánzàng** (玄奘, 602–664). Xuánzàng brought it back to China, translated its key texts, and with his disciple Kuījī (窺基) established the Chinese school known as 法相宗 (the "dharma-characteristics" school) or 唯識宗. Yogācāra thought also passed into Tibet, where it remains part of the standard curriculum.

Yogācāra did not see itself as rejecting Madhyamaka. It accepted emptiness, but it held that "emptiness" can be misread as sheer nothingness, and it set out to explain *how* experience arises, *why* we misperceive it, and *what* is transformed when we awaken. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* (《解深密經》), the school's chief scripture, calls this the "third turning of the wheel of Dharma", a teaching that makes explicit what the earlier teaching of emptiness left implicit.

The scriptural root of the phrase "consciousness-only" is a conversation in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, in the chapter on analysing yoga (分別瑜伽品). The bodhisattva Maitreya asks the Buddha about the image (影像) that a meditator sees in concentration: is it different from the mind that sees it, or not? The Buddha answers that it is not different, and adds: "I teach that the object of consciousness is merely what consciousness manifests" (我說識所緣，唯識所現故).

This is a meditator's observation before it is a philosophical thesis. In samādhi one can call up a skeleton, a disc of colour, or a Buddha-image; it appears vividly and is clearly "there", yet it is plainly produced by the mind. Yogācāra asks us to look at ordinary waking experience in the same light. What we take to be a world of independent things "out there", grasped by a self "in here", is a structured appearance arising within consciousness, conditioned by past habit.

**1. Eight consciousnesses.** Earlier Abhidharma counted six consciousnesses (識, *vijñāna*): eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness. Yogācāra adds two deeper layers, giving **eight consciousnesses** (八識):

items: the five sense consciousnesses (前五識), each knowing only its own kind of object, only in the present;
the **mental consciousness** (意識, *mano-vijñāna*), which thinks, remembers, names, and judges, and which is the main agent of karma;
the **manas** (末那識), a subtle, constant self-reference that takes the eighth consciousness to be "I";
the **ālayavijñāna** (阿賴耶識, "storehouse consciousness"), the underlying stream that holds the seeds of all experience, sustains the body, and carries a being from life to life.

blocks.text: You will meet the first six in detail in fascicle 1, and the ālayavijñāna is named in its very first pages as the "seed support" of every consciousness.

**2. Seeds and perfuming.** Every intentional act, even a moment of seeing coloured by liking or disliking, leaves an impression in the ālayavijñāna. This is called **perfuming** (熏習, *vāsanā*): as incense scents a cloth without leaving any visible mark, so experience leaves a latent trace. The traces are called **seeds** (種子, *bīja*). When conditions come together, seeds ripen into new experience, which in turn perfumes new seeds. This cycle explains memory, character, and karma without positing a permanent self.
**3. The three natures.** Yogācāra describes every phenomenon under three aspects, the **three natures** (三自性, *trisvabhāva*):

items: the **imagined nature** (遍計所執性, *parikalpita*): things as we construct and cling to them, as enduring, independent objects and selves. This aspect is not real at all;
the **dependent nature** (依他起性, *paratantra*): the flow of experience itself, arising from causes and conditions. This exists conventionally, as a process;
the **perfected nature** (圓成實性, *pariniṣpanna*): the dependent nature seen free of the imagined nature. This is suchness (真如, *tathatā*), the true character of things.

blocks.text: The classic image is a rope seen in the dark as a snake. The snake is imagined; the rope, depending on its strands, is dependent; seeing that there never was a snake is the perfected. The same three are also described negatively as the "three non-natures" (三無性), which is how Yogācāra keeps faith with the Madhyamaka teaching of emptiness.

**4. Transformation of the basis.** The goal is not merely to understand this analysis but to undergo **transformation of the basis** (轉依, *āśraya-parāvṛtti*): the defiled seeds in the ālayavijñāna are eliminated and the pure seeds are developed until the eight consciousnesses are turned into the **four wisdoms** (四智). The ālayavijñāna becomes the great mirror wisdom (大圓鏡智); the manas, the wisdom of equality (平等性智); the mental consciousness, the wisdom of wondrous observation (妙觀察智); and the five sense consciousnesses, the wisdom that accomplishes what is to be done (成所作智). The path towards this is mapped in **five stages** (五位): accumulation, preparation, seeing, cultivation, and completion.
Western books often call Yogācāra a form of idealism. There is truth in this, but it needs care.

Yogācāra does deny that objects exist *independently of* consciousness; Vasubandhu's *Twenty Verses* argue the point with the example of dreams. But it does not say that consciousness is a permanent, self-existent substance. Consciousness too is dependently arisen, momentary, and empty of own-nature; clinging to "consciousness" as ultimately real is itself a form of grasping that must be abandoned. "Only" is a method for removing the belief in external, independent things and selves. It is not an invitation to set up "mind" as a new absolute.

It also helps to know what to expect from our treatise. Much of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, especially its Basic Section, which we read first, speaks in the realistic language of Abhidharma. It talks of the four great elements, of form "with obstruction", of the world's formation and destruction. The sharpest "consciousness-only" arguments come later, in the *Compendium of Ascertainments* and in works such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Cheng Weishi Lun*. The treatise lays the descriptive groundwork; the later texts draw out its philosophical implications.
A few practical points for our daily sessions:

items: **It is a map, not a story.** The text proceeds by question and answer and by numbered lists: "What is X? It is fivefold: …" Read slowly, and keep track of where each list sits in the larger structure.

**The outline matters.** Chinese commentators divide the text into a nested outline (科判) using the characters 甲乙丙丁…. Each day's notes show where we are in that outline, so that the lists do not become a blur.

**Terms are precise.** The same English word may render two different Chinese terms, and vice versa. Each term is given in Chinese, Sanskrit, and English the first time it appears, and the Glossary keeps them together.

**It is meant to be practised.** Our teachers repeatedly point out that the analysis of the five sense consciousnesses is not trivia: seeing how a single moment of seeing is assembled from conditions is already insight into non-self (無我, *anātman*).

blocks.text: Tomorrow's introduction looks at the *Yogācārabhūmi* itself: who taught it, how it is organised, and why Xuánzàng travelled to India to obtain it.

quiz.q: Xuánzàng's term 唯識 renders which Sanskrit expression?
quiz.why: 唯識 renders *vijñapti-mātra*, "nothing but representation". *Citta-mātra* (唯心, "mind-only") is a related scriptural phrase, which is one reason "Mind-Only" is a loose name for this school.

quiz.q: What does the name "Yogācāra" literally refer to?
options: The study of logic and debate
The practice of yoga, that is, meditative discipline
The doctrine of the three natures
quiz.why: *Yogācāra* means "practice of yoga". The school is named after its method, and our treatise, the *Yogācārabhūmi*, is "the stages of the yoga practitioner".

quiz.q: In the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, what does the Buddha say about the image a meditator sees in concentration?
options: It is an external object reflected in the mind.
It is a sign sent by the Buddhas.
It is not different from the mind; the object of consciousness is merely what consciousness manifests.
It is unreal and should be ignored.
quiz.why: "I teach that the object of consciousness is merely what consciousness manifests" (我說識所緣，唯識所現故). This meditative observation is the scriptural root of "consciousness-only".

quiz.q: Which of the eight consciousnesses holds the seeds of all experience?
quiz.why: The ālayavijñāna (阿賴耶識) is the "storehouse" in which seeds are perfumed, held, and ripened. In fascicle 1 it is named as the "seed support" of the eye-consciousness.

quiz.q: In the rope-and-snake image, the snake corresponds to which nature?
quiz.why: The snake was never there: it is the imagined nature (遍計所執性). The rope, arising from its strands, is the dependent nature; seeing that no snake was ever there corresponds to the perfected nature.
